studies.title: Relational Operant Skills Training Increases Standardized Matrices Scores in Adolescents: A Stratified Active-Controlled Trial
studies.authors: McLoughlin, S., Tyndall, I., & Pereira, A.
studies.feature: Derive new relations between unfamiliar symbols: reverse a comparison correctly, connect a chain of premises, and follow the relational cue instead of surface familiarity.
studies.positiveFinding: In a three-month school study, SMART relational training produced a larger improvement on a standardized matrix-reasoning measure than Scratch coding. The final matrix analysis included 43 SMART and 27 coding participants. The training practiced same/opposite and more/less relations using new nonsense syllables and progressively more complex networks.
studies.limitation: Classes were not randomly assigned; substantial missing data and different incentives constrain the inference. The programs did not differ in processing-speed improvement. Published online in 2020.

studies.title: Can SMART Training Really Increase Intelligence? A Replication Study
studies.authors: Colbert, D., Tyndall, I., Roche, B., & Cassidy, S.
studies.feature: Practice relational rules repeatedly across examples and test whether improved reasoning extends beyond the trained symbol sets.
studies.positiveFinding: Twenty-six secondary-school students were divided into groups matched on initial IQ. After 12 weeks of SMART training, assessments by testers blind to group membership found training effects on Verbal IQ, Matrix Reasoning and Vocabulary. This provides another positive controlled precedent for relational-skills practice.
studies.limitation: This was a small matched-group study. Its specific positive test results do not establish a universal increase across every ability or validate the app's ontology operators.

studies.title: Processing capacity defined by relational complexity: Implications for comparative, developmental, and cognitive psychology
studies.authors: Halford, G. S., Wilson, W. H., & Phillips, S.
studies.feature: Distinguish the number of words or premises from the relationships that must be coordinated at once; organize a complex imagined world into meaningful parts without losing their connections.
studies.positiveFinding: This account links reasoning demands to the dimensions of a relation processed together. It explains how segmentation and conceptual chunking can make complex structures manageable. The framework gives a principled rationale for practicing integrated relations and building larger systems from understood components.
studies.limitation: A theoretical account of how processing demands depend on coordinated relationships. Its contribution is a way to describe and organize complexity; training outcomes require intervention evidence.

studies.title: Inductive Reasoning: A Training Approach
studies.authors: Klauer, K. J., & Phye, G. D.
studies.feature: Learn a deliberate comparison strategy: identify what stays the same, what changes, and which relationship explains a pattern.
studies.positiveFinding: This review and meta-analysis combined 74 training experiments involving nearly 3,600 children. It reported positive transfer from an explicit inductive-reasoning strategy to intelligence-test performance and academic learning, with stronger transfer to academic learning. It offers substantial positive precedent for teaching a reusable reasoning procedure.
studies.limitation: The findings concern a specific family of child-focused instructional programs; the same effect size cannot be assumed for independent adult play.

studies.title: Differential effects of reasoning and speed training in children
studies.authors: Mackey, A. P., Hill, S. S., Stone, S. I., & Bunge, S. A.
studies.feature: Combining several relations, planning a solution, and practicing reasoning with varied problems.
studies.positiveFinding: After eight weeks of board and computer games, children aged 7–9 in the reasoning program improved on an untrained nonverbal reasoning test. A separate speed program preferentially improved processing speed. This is positive intervention evidence that the content of practice can matter for the ability that improves.
studies.limitation: The intervention combined several games in schoolchildren; it does not isolate any one feature of either mode.

studies.title: Relational Integration Training Modulated the Frontoparietal Network for Fluid Intelligence: An EEG Microstates Study
studies.authors: Wang, Z., Sun, T., & Xiao, F.
studies.feature: Relational integration as a trainable target: holding several relationships together to answer a new question.
studies.positiveFinding: A randomized month-long study compared relational-integration training with an active control group (29 versus 28 participants), using matrix reasoning and resting EEG. The reported training-related changes included EEG dynamics associated with frontoparietal processing. This is a close intervention precedent for investigating relational integration, rather than only simple item memory.
studies.limitation: The accessible abstract emphasizes neural outcomes; it does not establish a durable behavioral effect size or validate these modes.

studies.title: The relational integration task explains fluid reasoning above and beyond other working memory tasks
studies.authors: Chuderski, A.
studies.feature: Binding the correct entity to its relation, endpoint, category and scope; keeping several bindings available at once.
studies.positiveFinding: Across three studies, relational-integration performance was sensitive to the number of bindings and explained fluid-reasoning differences beyond several other memory and attention measures. The findings make accurate relation binding a well-motivated target for complex reasoning practice.
studies.limitation: The link to fluid reasoning is correlational. Extra words or distractors do not automatically create greater relational integration.

studies.title: Learning and transfer: A general role for analogical encoding
studies.authors: Gentner, D., Loewenstein, J., & Thompson, L.
studies.feature: The Da Vinci method: explicitly compare different imagined domains while preserving who plays each role and how the relations fit together.
studies.positiveFinding: Learners who compared analogous negotiation cases abstracted their shared structure and transferred the principle to new problems more successfully than learners who studied the cases separately. Experiments included transfer to a subsequent face-to-face negotiation. Deliberate comparison can make a useful pattern portable across different surface stories.
studies.limitation: The measured transfer concerned negotiation principles. The tested learning procedure involved explicitly comparing cases and abstracting their shared structure.

studies.title: Learning by Analogical Bootstrapping
studies.authors: Kurtz, K. J., Miao, C.-H., & Gentner, D.
studies.feature: Build concrete embodiments of an abstract relation, then explain the corresponding objects, processes and causal links.
studies.positiveFinding: Comparing two partly understood heat-flow situations helped learners discover a common causal structure. Prompts that supported joint interpretation and explicit correspondences were especially useful. This supports making the cross-domain exercise an active explanation of what corresponds to what.
studies.limitation: These were science-comprehension experiments. Extending the method to repeated ontology-world practice is a design hypothesis.

studies.title: Structure-Mapping: A Theoretical Framework for Analogy
studies.authors: Gentner, D.
studies.feature: Keep entity correspondences consistent and connect relations into larger systems, including relations between relations.
studies.positiveFinding: Structure-mapping theory explains analogy through shared relational organization across domains. Its systematicity principle favors connected higher-order structure. This gives the Da Vinci method a precise design rationale: preserve the pattern of relationships while changing the concrete world used to imagine it.
studies.limitation: A theoretical framework for analogy and systematic relational correspondence. It supplies design principles for organizing the comparison; the game’s category system is an application of those principles.

studies.title: Relational language and the development of relational mapping
studies.authors: Loewenstein, J., & Gentner, D.
studies.feature: Use meaningful labels to identify relational correspondence despite competing object resemblance. In the imagined worlds, define each role clearly and explain which entity fills it in each domain.
studies.positiveFinding: In five experiments, spatial relational language helped preschool children map corresponding positions between structures. The meanings of the terms mattered, and one experiment found an advantage two days later without additional labels. Language can help a learner notice a relational organization that surface appearances obscure.
studies.limitation: The studies used children's spatial vocabulary. Applying this scaffold to Inner/Outer or other custom operators requires clear operational definitions.

studies.title: Comparison in the Development of Categories
studies.authors: Gentner, D., & Namy, L. L.
studies.feature: Recognize a common category across different embodiments and resist a tempting match based only on appearance.
studies.positiveFinding: Four-year-olds who compared multiple examples with a shared label were more likely to choose a taxonomic category match over a perceptually similar alternative. Comparison helped them move beyond obvious surface resemblance. This supports using contrasting embodiments to teach what an operator means.
studies.limitation: Category-learning experiments with four-year-olds. The application to adult practice carries over the operation of comparing embodiments to discover a common category.

studies.title: An episodic specificity induction enhances means-end problem solving in young and older adults
studies.authors: Madore, K. P., & Schacter, D. L.
studies.feature: Make an imagined world specific: identify the entities, setting, event sequence and relevant steps connecting a situation to a goal.
studies.positiveFinding: A brief induction encouraging detailed recollection increased relevant solution steps and episodic detail during means-end problem solving in both young and older adults. The improvement was selective rather than a general increase in irrelevant content. Detailed mental simulation can contribute useful material to solving a problem.
studies.limitation: A brief induction with immediate problem-solving outcomes in young and older adults. It provides evidence about detailed simulation during problem solving; sustained practice is a further application.

studies.title: Creativity and Memory: Effects of an Episodic-Specificity Induction on Divergent Thinking
studies.authors: Madore, K. P., Addis, D. R., & Schacter, D. L.
studies.feature: Generate fresh concrete interpretations of the same abstract structure instead of recycling one familiar story.
studies.positiveFinding: In two experiments, a brief induction focused on episodic detail improved divergent thinking on an unusual-uses task. The selective result supports a connection between detailed memory construction and generating alternative ideas—a useful component of varied cross-domain imagination.
studies.limitation: Benefits did not extend to all comparison tasks. Divergent idea generation is a different outcome from convergent reasoning or fluid intelligence.

studies.title: A counterfactual simulation model of causal judgments for physical events
studies.authors: Gerstenberg, T., Goodman, N. D., Lagnado, D. A., & Tenenbaum, J. B.
studies.feature: Give the imagined world a stated mechanism, then ask what would change if an entity or interaction were altered.
studies.positiveFinding: Across experiments with physical events, a model that simulated alternative possibilities explained causal judgments better than accounts based only on what actually happened. Identical actual events could receive different judgments when their counterfactual possibilities differed. This supports making imagined alternatives precise enough to reason about.
studies.limitation: Mechanism experiments on causal judgment. Applying them here means explicitly supplying a causal rule within the imagined world and evaluating what changes under an intervention.

studies.title: Problem-oriented training promotes spontaneous analogical transfer: Memory-oriented training promotes memory for training
studies.authors: Needham, D. R., & Begg, I. M.
studies.feature: Try to reconstruct or explain the relationship before checking the answer, then use the correct explanation to improve the next attempt.
studies.positiveFinding: Across five experiments, attempting to solve a problem or explain a situation before seeing its solution promoted spontaneous analogical transfer more than approaching the material mainly as something to remember. Even initially unsuccessful attempts could help when followed by the solution.
studies.limitation: Transfer was measured between problems over short intervals. The practical connection is active reconstruction followed by applying the learned relationship to another problem.

studies.title: Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing
studies.authors: Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L., III
studies.feature: After a response, review the correct relationship and identify the misleading alternative, especially when lures look almost right.
studies.positiveFinding: Both immediate and delayed corrective feedback improved later recall and reduced intrusion of incorrect multiple-choice alternatives compared with testing without feedback. Feedback can therefore help practice strengthen correct knowledge while preventing attractive errors from being rehearsed.
studies.limitation: This was factual learning, not intelligence training. Its strongest application here is to explanatory correction, beyond a correct/incorrect signal alone.

studies.title: On the acquisition of abstract knowledge: Structural alignment and explication in learning causal system categories
studies.authors: Goldwater, M. B., & Gentner, D.
studies.feature: Explain a concrete world, then explicitly map its roles and relations onto a different domain. Use a category to express a repeatable system pattern rather than merely memorizing its name.
studies.positiveFinding: Explaining individual examples improved their representation; comparing analogous examples improved recognition of causal patterns across new domains. Combining explanation with explicit correspondence mapping produced the strongest generalization. This is a close positive precedent for the explanation-and-transfer steps of Da Vinci practice.
studies.limitation: The outcomes concerned recognizing causal-system categories, including common cause and feedback. Apply the comparison procedure to explicitly defined roles and mechanisms in each imagined domain.

studies.title: Learning of role-governed and thematic categories
studies.authors: Goldwater, M. B., Bainbridge, R., & Murphy, G. L.
studies.feature: Identify what an entity does within a relationship. For example, distinguish a connecting hub from a connected endpoint, then embody that role with different objects while retaining the game's category definitions.
studies.positiveFinding: Across five experiments using short action films, people formed categories around shared roles even with few perceptual or linguistic cues. Comparison helped them recognize more abstract roles across different actions that they had not grouped together spontaneously.
studies.limitation: Experiments on relational category learning. Their comparison and role-interpretation procedures motivate giving each category a concrete job and recognizing that job across different embodiments.

studies.title: Relational discovery in category learning
studies.authors: Goldwater, M. B., Don, H. J., Krusche, M. J. F., & Livesey, E. J.
studies.feature: Actively infer the missing relationship before checking it. In a practice break, reconstruct the endpoint direction and explain the pattern that stays fixed when the imagined domain changes.
studies.positiveFinding: Experiments separated surface features from the relations defining artificial categories. Learning by inferring missing parts helped learners discover the relational rule and apply it to perceptually different examples, including learners not initially inclined to discover rules.
studies.limitation: The transfer phase included corrective feedback, so the result also concerns preparation for further learning. Benefits of other task manipulations depended on learners' strategies; this was not a test of broad intelligence change.

studies.title: Far-Out Thinking: Generating Solutions to Distant Analogies Promotes Relational Thinking
studies.authors: Vendetti, M. S., Wu, A., & Holyoak, K. J.
studies.feature: Actively generate a structurally correct analogy in a different domain, then return to the exact entity-to-role mapping. Producing the correspondence is a more specific exercise than merely recognizing a supplied story.
studies.positiveFinding: Generating solutions to distant verbal analogies increased relational choices on a later, unrelated picture-mapping task, even after accounting for fluid intelligence and response time. Evaluating supplied analogies and solving near analogies did not produce the same transfer. This closely supports the generative, cross-domain part of the Da Vinci method.
studies.limitation: An immediate shift toward relational mapping on a subsequent task. It supports the generative operation within Da Vinci practice; its persistence over extended training remains a research question.

studies.title: Generating distant analogies facilitates relational integration: Intermediary role of relational mindset and cognitive load
studies.authors: Du, X., & Sun, P.
studies.feature: Use a brief, actively constructed distant analogy before integrating several premises. In the practice break, say which objects correspond and why their relationships match before solving the combined world.
studies.positiveFinding: Laboratory experiments connected distant-analogy generation with better subsequent relational integration. Benefits included higher scores than near-analogy generation on premise-integration and Latin-square tasks, and higher multidimensional reasoning scores than analogy evaluation. In a statistics-learning experiment, the generation group responded faster and showed better concept mastery without a significant accuracy difference.
studies.limitation: The two initial tasks did not show significant generation advantages over their control groups in the reported overall comparisons. These are immediate priming and learning effects; persistence, the mediation mechanism and this app's combined training remain open questions.

studies.title: Effects of generating versus evaluating distant analogies on subsequent relational integration: mediating and moderating mechanisms
studies.authors: Du, X., & Sun, P.
studies.feature: A second close precedent for generating a distant analogy before a demanding relationship problem: build the mapping yourself, then test the world using its actual premises.
studies.positiveFinding: In a randomized study of 120 Chinese college students, the analogy-generation group outperformed the analogy-evaluation group on a subsequent multidimensional relational reasoning task. The generation group also reported lower cognitive load. The advantage was more evident among participants with lower measured working-memory capacity.
studies.limitation: Published in August 2026 by the same authors as the 2022 study. A single-session experiment with an active comparison and immediate reasoning outcomes. Cognitive-load mediation used self-reports and remains a proposed explanation.

studies.title: Generating distant analogies increases metaphor production
studies.authors: George, T., Christofalos, A. L., & Pambuccian, F. S.
studies.feature: Invent a compact metaphor that preserves several relevant features of a world. Explain the shared relations so that a creative label does real representational work.
studies.positiveFinding: After solving cross-domain rather than within-domain analogies, participants more often used metaphors to summarize new topics. Metaphors were also more frequent when the topic supplied several features to integrate. The result provides an additional bridge from distant analogy to flexible, abstract expression.
studies.limitation: The measured outcome was metaphor production. Its application here combines creative description with a separate check that the intended roles and relationships remain consistent.

studies.title: Schema induction and analogical transfer
studies.authors: Gick, M. L., & Holyoak, K. J.
studies.feature: Compare two concrete worlds with the same organization and state their common rule. Preserve one consistent mapping when names, wording and imagined domains change.
studies.positiveFinding: Learners who described similarities between two analogous stories often extracted a general solution structure that supported transfer to a different problem. The quality of that extracted structure predicted transfer. Verbal principles and diagrams became useful supports when paired with two examples, even though they had achieved little with only one.
studies.limitation: The experiments measured transfer of a particular problem-solving schema. Learners compared the underlying relationships across examples to extract that schema.

studies.title: Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H.
studies.feature: Explain why a conclusion follows, which endpoint carries each aspect, and why a tempting alternative fails. Use the guide or practice feedback to check the explanation rather than merely repeating the answer.
studies.positiveFinding: Across 64 research reports contributing 69 effect sizes, prompts to explain causal or conceptual relationships improved learning with a weighted mean effect of g = 0.55. Benefits across instructional conditions support making explanatory reasoning an active part of practice.
studies.limitation: The average effect summarizes learning outcomes across varied instructional studies. Prompt content and instructional support matter when applying self-explanation to a new task.

studies.title: Forests or trees? The effect of generating solutions to distant analogies on global–local processing
studies.authors: Li, J., Shi, K., Cui, T., Gao, J., & Wei, X.
studies.feature: Consider the organization of the whole world as well as its individual endpoint details. A proposed practice extension is to describe the overall pattern first, then verify every local binding.
studies.positiveFinding: In two experiments, generating distant rather than near analogies increased global-pattern choices on the Kimchi–Palmer task and accelerated responses to global letters on the Navon task. This suggests that distant-analogy work can influence how later visual information is organized.
studies.limitation: Global visual processing is different from coordinating nested semantic worlds, and a global preference is not always better than attention to detail. The paper was published online in 2023 and appeared in a 2024 issue.

studies.title: Innovation Relies on the Obscure: A Key to Overcoming the Classic Problem of Functional Fixedness
studies.authors: McCaffrey, T.
studies.feature: When imagining a new embodiment, look beyond an object's familiar name or use. Consider its parts and relevant properties so the same entity can play a different, explicitly justified role.
studies.positiveFinding: Training in a generic-parts technique helped participants notice overlooked features and solve more insight problems than a control group. The finding supplies a concrete positive precedent for deliberately changing an object's representation to overcome functional fixedness.
studies.limitation: The tested strategy addressed object-use insight problems. The connection to imagined worlds is actively examining parts and properties and explaining how they enable a different role.

studies.title: The Mental Models Training App: Enhancing verbal reasoning through a cognitive training mobile application
studies.authors: Cortes, R. A., Weinberger, A. B., & Green, A. E.
studies.feature: Combine given premises, derive their consequence and check the candidate conclusion. This is the inference operation that Da Vinci practice can pair with generating worlds and explaining corresponding roles.
studies.positiveFinding: In a preregistered randomized study with 301 analyzed adults, app-based reasoning practice improved immediate deductive-reasoning accuracy and response time compared with no intervention. During training, an external spatial-modeling tool helped participants pass difficult three-premise problems in fewer attempts. This is a close positive precedent for practicing the modes' inference component.
studies.limitation: The modeling app did not outperform active reasoning-practice controls on the posttest. The study tested one session and immediate outcomes, so it supports reasoning practice without establishing an additional visualization benefit, lasting gains or transfer to general intelligence.

studies.title: What Makes Mental Modeling Difficult? Normative Data for the Multidimensional Relational Reasoning Task
studies.authors: Cortes, R. A., Weinberger, A. B., Colaizzi, G. A., Porter, G. F., Dyke, E. L., Keaton, H. O., Walker, D. L., & Green, A. E.
studies.feature: Identify how many relations must be held together to solve a problem. Apply this task-analysis approach when selecting a manageable level of premise integration and when explaining what makes a particular world difficult.
studies.positiveFinding: In 310 adults, systematically varying relational problems showed that additional premises and multidimensional relations made reasoning more difficult. The authors released the problems and normative data, providing a useful empirical benchmark for identifying which parts of a task demand more relational processing.
studies.limitation: This is task-design evidence, not a training-benefit trial: harder does not automatically mean more effective. The study did not compare this game's direction resolutions, N-back delays or equal-step vector convention.

studies.title: A hierarchy for relational reasoning in the prefrontal cortex
studies.authors: Krawczyk, D. C., McClelland, M. M., & Donovan, C. M.
studies.feature: Coordinate several relationships into one structure and compare that structure across formats. In Mode 2, nested worlds add relations between whole substructures; cross-domain imagination changes the objects while retaining relational organization.
studies.positiveFinding: An fMRI experiment compared visuospatial reasoning and verbal analogies within one study. Integrating more visuospatial relations recruited progressively anterior prefrontal regions, and analogical reasoning recruited overlapping regions more strongly than semantic and perceptual controls. This supplies converging mechanism evidence that different-looking reasoning tasks can share relational-integration processes.
studies.limitation: Brain-imaging evidence about the mechanisms used during integration and analogy. Nested ontology worlds are a proposed application of this organization principle; the experiment measured task-related recruitment.

studies.title: Frontopolar Cortex Specializes for Manipulation of Structured Information
studies.authors: Kroger, J., & Kim, C.
studies.feature: Keep each property attached to its correct entity, then deliberately transform the structured model. This relates to Mode 2's endpoint bindings and practice question that changes premise directions while retaining the entities and descriptors.
studies.positiveFinding: The article reports an fMRI experiment with 15 adults that separated maintaining bound information from changing it. Manipulating letters whose identities, colors and locations were linked recruited frontopolar cortex more than maintaining a larger bound set. The result supports treating structured transformation as a distinct cognitive demand rather than merely adding more items to remember.
studies.limitation: A small mechanism experiment using bound letter identities, colors and locations. The proposed application carries over deliberate transformation of a bound structure to semantic roles.

studies.title: Solving distant analogies reduces belief-based responding in transitive inference
studies.authors: Andrews, G., & Vann, D. M.
studies.feature: Follow the given relationships even when familiar meanings suggest a different answer. Cross-domain comparison can serve as a cue to check structure; in Mode 2, an evocative category name must stay attached to the exact endpoint specified by the problem.
studies.positiveFinding: After generating solutions to distant rather than near analogies, participants showed less belief-based responding on subsequent transitive-inference problems. The authors reported elimination of the observed belief-based response pattern and better relational responding when a valid conclusion conflicted with familiar real-world beliefs. This connects cross-domain analogy with resisting a specific reasoning lure.
studies.limitation: An immediate effect on belief-sensitive transitive inference. A broader inhibitory-control explanation was proposed; the measured result concerned responding on that particular reasoning task.

studies.title: Comparison and Categorization in the Development of Relational Similarity
studies.authors: Kotovsky, L., & Gentner, D.
studies.feature: Build a bridge toward distant analogies: first make the shared relationship clear in familiar examples, then preserve that relationship across increasingly different domains.
studies.positiveFinding: Across four developmental experiments, comparison and category learning helped children recognize abstract relational commonalities. Four-year-olds who successfully compared patterns within both size and colour dimensions subsequently recognized corresponding relations across those dimensions; practice confined to size comparisons offered less support. A further training study improved cross-dimensional matching after children learned the component comparisons.
studies.limitation: The learning studies involved small samples of four-year-olds and immediate pattern-matching outcomes. Successful alignment of the easier relations was an important condition for the benefit.

studies.title: The Transfer of Scientific Principles Using Concrete and Idealized Simulations
studies.authors: Goldstone, R. L., & Son, J. Y.
studies.feature: Use a vivid imagined example to understand the roles, then express its rule compactly before rebuilding it in a different domain: concrete example → relational rule → new example.
studies.positiveFinding: In two experiments with interactive scientific simulations, participants transferred understanding of the same competitive-specialization principle between different settings. Starting with concrete elements and then simplifying their appearance produced the best transfer, outperforming consistently concrete, consistently abstract and reverse-order presentations. Both changing-format conditions outperformed keeping one format throughout.
studies.limitation: The measured benefit concerned learning and transfer between two simulations with a shared scientific principle. Applying that progression to self-generated imagination is a practice-design inference.

studies.title: Converging on a new role for analogy in problem solving and retrieval: When two problems are better than one
studies.authors: Kurtz, K. J., & Loewenstein, J.
studies.feature: When a relationship feels hard to interpret, compare two unfinished situations with the same constraints; their common structure can help retrieve a useful earlier example.
studies.positiveFinding: Three experiments found that comparing two unsolved problems helped participants retrieve and apply a previously studied analogous solution. In the first experiment, 54% produced the convergence solution after target comparison, versus 15% after one target. The second experiment separated genuine comparison from simply solving two problems; explicit comparison improved solutions over separate attempts.
studies.limitation: These were immediate undergraduate problem-solving experiments using convergence stories. The third experiment specifically supported retrieval of a prior example as part of the effect.

studies.title: Reviving Inert Knowledge: Analogical Abstraction Supports Relational Retrieval of Past Events
studies.authors: Gentner, D., Loewenstein, J., Thompson, L., & Forbus, K. D.
studies.feature: After comparing your two imagined domains, state their common rule and search your own experience for a third situation with that structure.
studies.positiveFinding: Five experiments showed that comparing analogous cases improved retrieval of structurally matching examples. The effect appeared both in memories from participants' own lives and in controlled laboratory material. Management consultants and students who compared negotiation cases retrieved better matching experiences than those studying cases separately. The first experiment also found improved use of the principle in a later negotiation.
studies.limitation: The experiments assessed prompted retrieval and specific problem transfer. The life-experience studies relied on participants' reported memories, alongside later experiments with controlled memory sets.

studies.title: Does Comparing Solution Methods Facilitate Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge? An Experimental Study on Learning to Solve Equations
studies.authors: Rittle-Johnson, B., & Star, J. R.
studies.feature: Compare two valid ways to reach the same conclusion. Explain which relations each method uses and when one makes the reasoning easier to follow.
studies.positiveFinding: Seventy seventh-grade students were randomly assigned to compare alternative algebra solutions or study the same methods separately. Comparison produced greater gains in procedural knowledge and flexibility, including applying methods to unfamiliar equations. The advantage concerned explicitly examining similarities and differences between methods, beyond exposure to multiple solutions.
studies.limitation: Students attended one selective private school. Conceptual-knowledge gains were comparable between groups; the clearest advantage concerned procedures and flexible strategy use.

studies.title: The Role of Explanation in Discovery and Generalization: Evidence From Category Learning
studies.authors: Williams, J. J., & Lombrozo, T.
studies.feature: After creating examples, explain which common rule makes them belong together. Use the explanation to notice a relation that survives changes in objects and setting.
studies.positiveFinding: Across three category-learning experiments, explaining category membership made adults more likely to discover the broad rule than describing examples, thinking aloud, or studying freely. Results also suggested a role for explaining unusual cases when revising an initial rule.
studies.limitation: The experiments measured discovery and generalization of artificial category rules. Describing examples better preserved individual details in the first experiment, making a separate detail check useful alongside abstraction.

studies.title: Explanation recruits comparison in a category-learning task
studies.authors: Edwards, B. J., Williams, J. J., Gentner, D., & Lombrozo, T.
studies.feature: Compare a small family of examples for a proposed relation. Ask what explains every member, then test the proposed rule against a contrasting case.
studies.positiveFinding: Three experiments with adults learning artificial robot categories connected explanation with stronger rule discovery. In the second experiment, comparing whole groups of category members supported rule learning better than comparing isolated pairs. Self-reported group comparison partly accounted for the explanation benefit in the third experiment.
studies.limitation: Study periods were brief and time-matched within experiments. The proposed mediation used self-report; the central outcome was identifying the category rule.

studies.title: Ask me why, don’t tell me why: Asking children for explanations facilitates relational thinking
studies.authors: Brockbank, E., Lombrozo, T., Gopnik, A., & Walker, C. M.
studies.feature: Explain why two examples share a relationship before comparing their appearance. In Mode 2, give each category role a plain-language reason and preserve that role in the second imagined domain.
studies.positiveFinding: Forty-six 5- and 6-year-olds were randomly assigned to explain demonstrated matches or report the observed choice. Explainers reliably chose relational matches over look-alike object matches across subsequent trials, while the reporting group favored the object matches.
studies.limitation: This was a single-session developmental study using same-relation shape pairs. The article appeared online in 2022 and in the 2023 journal volume.

studies.title: Explaining the moral of the story
studies.authors: Walker, C. M., & Lombrozo, T.
studies.feature: Build an imagined scene around a rule, explain why events illustrate that rule, then carry the rule into a new scene with different characters and objects.
studies.positiveFinding: Two experiments with 5- and 6-year-olds found that explaining story events helped children extract an underlying lesson and recognize it in new contexts despite distracting surface similarities. In some comparisons, generating the explanation was more effective than being explicitly told the lesson.
studies.limitation: The randomized experiments involved 48 and 96 children and immediate story-comprehension tasks. The measured transfer concerned the story lesson and its application to new vignettes.

studies.title: Thought Experiments as an Error Detection and Correction Tool
studies.authors: Bascandziev, I.
studies.feature: Use a thought experiment to expose incompatible predictions. Compare the imagined result with the rule you first proposed, then repair the explanation that caused the conflict.
studies.positiveFinding: In an adult experiment with 575 analyzed participants, bodily thought experiments paired with comparison or argument prompts improved immediate force-and-motion judgments; the baseline sequence of thought experiments showed no significant improvement. The prompts connected familiar experiences with participants’ earlier answers.
studies.limitation: A second experiment with 574 adults used external-object versions: improvement was smaller and the conditions did not differ significantly. The findings favor carefully chosen scenarios plus explicit comparison; both experiments used immediate repeated-item assessments.

studies.title: Effects of explanation on children’s question asking
studies.authors: Ruggeri, A., Xu, F., & Lombrozo, T.
studies.feature: Turn an explanation into a useful next question: which relationship or shared feature would distinguish several possible interpretations? Apply this when checking an imagined analogy or category role.
studies.positiveFinding: Across two randomized experiments involving 168 children, explaining examples before a 20-questions game helped the older children, aged 6–7, solve it with fewer questions. They shifted away from asking about individual objects toward questions about shared features.
studies.limitation: The benefit was age-dependent and concerned subsequent information search within the same domain. Questioning improved without consistently shifting to the mathematically most efficient question at every step.

studies.title: Repeated Testing Produces Superior Transfer of Learning Relative to Repeated Studying
studies.authors: Butler, A. C.
studies.feature: Retrieve a relational principle, explain it, then apply it to a new imagined domain. In Da Vinci reflection, reconstruct the relationship before checking the example or inventing its counterpart.
studies.positiveFinding: Across four experiments, repeated testing with feedback improved retention and transfer relative to restudying. One week later, benefits extended to new inferential questions; the final experiment transferred concepts between knowledge domains. This supports a practice sequence that combines remembering a principle with using it in a different setting.
studies.limitation: Prose-learning experiments; cross-domain questions explicitly cued the relevant earlier concept. The demonstrated outcome was delayed application of learned knowledge. Feedback was part of the retrieval condition.

studies.title: Retrieval Practice Benefits Deductive Inference
studies.authors: Eglington, L. G., & Kang, S. H. K.
studies.feature: Build the connected model before rehearsing its pieces. For Mode 1, connect the premises before recalling the triad; for Mode 2, reconstruct who occupies each category role and how the roles relate.
studies.positiveFinding: Across three experiments, retrieval practice improved deductive inference two days later when related sentences were available together during study and practice. Both fill-in-the-blank retrieval and free recall outperformed rereading under this format. The findings connect memory practice with integration: learners benefit when practice allows relationships among facts to be processed.
studies.limitation: Participants learned sets of seven to nine related sentences. The benefit depended on presentation supporting relational processing; one-at-a-time presentation showed no inference advantage. Journal issue 2018; first published online in 2016.

studies.title: The importance of constructive comprehension processes in learning from tests
studies.authors: Hinze, S. R., Wiley, J., & Pellegrino, J. W.
studies.feature: During Da Vinci reflection, reconstruct why the relationships hold. Explain the connection between the two premises and the candidate, then explain how the same organization appears in another domain.
studies.positiveFinding: Experiments with science texts found that directing retrieval toward explanations produced more coherent responses and better performance one week later than rereading. Explanation quality predicted later learning beyond response length. This supports adding a meaningful why-and-how explanation to recalled relationships, rather than treating recall as a list of disconnected details.
studies.limitation: Delayed detail and inference tests assessed science-text learning. Experiment 3 included 93 students; explanation comparisons used one-tailed tests, including the smaller advantage over free recall. Application to game reflection is a design inference.

studies.title: Putting category learning in order: Category structure and temporal arrangement affect the benefit of interleaved over blocked study
studies.authors: Carvalho, P. F., & Goldstone, R. L.
studies.feature: Use two complementary comparisons in Da Vinci practice: varied examples sharing one relational rule, followed by a close alternative with a changed role. For Mode 2, this suggests contrasting easily confused category forms after finding examples of each.
studies.positiveFinding: Three category-learning experiments showed that practice order shaped generalization. Interleaving helped distinguish highly similar categories; blocked practice helped discover commonalities in less similar categories. This supplies a constructive rationale for choosing examples around the particular distinction being learned.
studies.limitation: The experiments used perceptual categories. Applying their commonality-versus-contrast principle to semantic ontology roles is a proposed learning strategy; the useful order depended on category structure.
